newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German builders agree minimum wage trial.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German builders agree minimum wage trial.

text.p: German construction trade union IG Bau said on Monday it had accepted employers' proposals of a generally-binding minimum wage for the industry that would last up until the end of August next year.

The agreement follows the failure of attempts earlier this year by IG Bau and industry associations to set a minimum wage for workers in the sector to stop widespread "wage-dumping" by foreign-owned contractors using cheaper labour.

A spokesman for IG Bau confirmed the minimum wage will be set at 17 marks for workers in western Germany and 15.64 for those in the east -- still some way down on the 18.60 marks and 17.11 marks respectively it had originally sought.

"The employers have however now moved a bit further forwards," IG Bau chairman Klaus Wiesehuegel said in a statement. Employers had originally wanted any minimum wage agreement to run until May 31 next year.
Wiesehuegel said it would now be possible to test minimum wages, and a related ruling that foreign-owned contractors also observe minimum wages, during part of the peak of the building season.

A previous wage agreement foundered in April after the BDA, the umbrella employers' federation for the industry, vetoed it, saying it exceeded lowest wages in other sectors and carried an inflationary risk.
Analysts generally played down concern that the agreement could hit contractor margins, despite noting that labour costing less than the minimum wage level now agreed was widely used.

"It suggests a reduction in margins, but not enough that it should affect investor decisions. It also takes some uncertainty out of the industry," said one Frankfurt analyst, who did not want to be named.

For the last five years, top German contractors such as Holsmann AG and Hochtief AG have had to contend with a generally disappointing market, which sector analysts do not expect to pick up much before 1998.
The building industry has estimated that low paying foreign firms, predominantly English and Portugese, employ around 200,000 foreign building workers in Germany.
They are widely blamed for the high unemployment rates among German construction workers, of whom around 200,000 are without jobs.
Industry groups have said that setting a minimum wage could help cut further employment losses.
IG Bau said it would now be calling on Germany's Federal Labour Office to make the necessary preparations to ensure the minimum wage was successfully implemented.
